questions.question: Which change has the largest increase in entropy of the system? Options: A H2O(s) -> H2O(l); B Hg(l) -> Hg(g); C H2O(l) + HCl(g) -> H3O+(aq) + Cl-(aq); D C(graphite) -> C(diamond).
questions.answer: B - Hg(l) -> Hg(g)
steps: Entropy rises most when a substance changes to a gas, because gas particles have far more positions and motion.
Option B is liquid to gas, the largest entropy increase of the four.
Option A (solid to liquid) gives a smaller increase.
Option C forms ions in solution from a gas, which is an ordering effect, so entropy does not rise greatly.
Option D (graphite to diamond) gives a decrease in entropy because diamond is more ordered.
So B is the answer.

questions.question: Which gas would have the greatest standard molar entropy? Options: A NH3, B H2, C N2, D SO2.
questions.answer: D - SO2
steps: Standard molar entropy increases with molar mass and number of atoms in the molecule.
SO2 has the largest molar mass (64) of the four gases and three atoms per molecule.
H2 has the smallest molar mass, so it has the lowest entropy of the four.
So SO2 has the greatest standard molar entropy, option D.

questions.question: Ammonium nitrate is very soluble in water. What is the best explanation? Options: A all ammonium salts are soluble, B activation energy is very low, C enthalpies of hydration are very exothermic, D deltaS system is positive.
questions.answer: D - the entropy change of the system is positive
steps: Ammonium nitrate is an ionic solid that dissolves to give separate ions in solution.
The ions become more dispersed, so the entropy of the system increases (deltaS positive).
A positive entropy change favours dissolution, even though the process is endothermic.
Option A is only a restatement, B concerns kinetics, and C is not the main reason, so D is the best explanation.

questions.question: What is the standard entropy change of the system, in J K-1 mol-1, for N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3? Options: A -198.8, B -129.9, C +129.9, D +198.8.
steps: Gas moles fall from 4 (1 N2 + 3 H2) to 2 (2 NH3), so entropy of the system decreases; the sign is negative.
This leaves options A and B, so the sign rules out C and D.
Using data book standard entropies (NH3 about 192.8, N2 about 191.6, H2 about 130.7 J K-1 mol-1): 2(192.8) - [191.6 + 3(130.7)] = about -198.
This magnitude matches option A (-198.8 J K-1 mol-1) rather than option B.

questions.question: Which substance has the highest standard molar entropy at 298 K and 1 atm? Options: A CO2, B Cu, C C2H5OH, D H2.
questions.answer: A - carbon dioxide, CO2(g)
steps: Gases have much higher entropy than liquids or solids.
Copper is a metallic solid, so it has low entropy; ethanol is a liquid, so it has lower entropy than any gas here.
Both CO2 and H2 are gases, but CO2 has a larger molar mass and more atoms, so it has the higher standard entropy.
So CO2 is the answer, option A.

questions.question: The standard molar entropy of a substance: A is not affected by state changes or temperature; B only changes with temperature; C only changes with state; D changes with temperature and with state change. Which is correct?
questions.answer: D - it changes both with temperature and with a change of state
steps: Entropy rises as temperature rises, because particles have more energy and motion.
Entropy also rises at a change of state (solid to liquid to gas), because particles become less ordered.
So standard molar entropy changes with both temperature and state, which is option D.

questions.question: In which series does the standard molar entropy of the compounds increase? Options: A CaO(s) < H2O(l) < CO2(g) < SO2(g); B CaO(s) < H2O(l) < SO2(g) < CO2(g); C SO2(g) < CO2(g) < H2O(l) < CaO(s); D CO2(g) < SO2(g) < H2O(l) < CaO(s).
questions.answer: A - CaO(s) < H2O(l) < CO2(g) < SO2(g)
steps: Solids have lower entropy than liquids, which have lower entropy than gases: CaO(s) lowest, H2O(l) next, then the gases.
Options C and D put gases before liquids/solids, so they are wrong.
Between CO2 and SO2 (both gases with three atoms), SO2 has the larger molar mass (64 vs 44), so SO2 has the higher entropy.
So the increasing order is CaO(s) < H2O(l) < CO2(g) < SO2(g), option A.

questions.question: Hydrogen and oxygen do not react until a platinum gauze is added, when the mixture explodes. In the absence of platinum, the mixture is: A kinetically stable and thermodynamically stable; B kinetically stable and thermodynamically unstable; C kinetically unstable and thermodynamically stable; D kinetically unstable and thermodynamically unstable.
questions.answer: B - kinetically stable and thermodynamically unstable
steps: Thermodynamic stability is about the energy of the products relative to the reactants: the reaction is exothermic and feasible, so the mixture is thermodynamically unstable.
Kinetic stability is about the rate: the reaction does not start without a catalyst, so the activation energy is high.
Platinum lowers the activation energy and the reaction proceeds rapidly.
So the mixture is kinetically stable and thermodynamically unstable, option B.

questions.question: Write the overall equation for the rapid decomposition of hydrogen peroxide catalysed by iodide ions, and state the role of the iodide ions.
questions.answer: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2; iodide ions are a catalyst (used in step 1 and regenerated in step 2)
steps: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes to water and oxygen: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2.
Iodide ions appear in the first step as a reactant and are regenerated in the second step.
A species that is used and then regenerated, and does not appear in the overall equation, is a catalyst.
So the iodide ions act as a catalyst, lowering the activation energy.

questions.question: Explain the formation of the blue-black colour in the clock reaction and why its appearance is delayed.
questions.answer: Iodine formed is reduced by thiosulfate, so no blue-black colour until all thiosulfate is used up; then iodine reacts with starch
steps: Iodine is formed by the reaction between hydrogen peroxide and iodide ions in acid.
Thiosulfate is added in a fixed amount and reduces the iodine as it forms: I2 + 2S2O3^2- -> 2I- + S4O6^2-.
While thiosulfate is present, iodine is removed as fast as it forms, so no iodine builds up.
When all the thiosulfate has been used, iodine accumulates and forms a blue-black starch-iodine complex.
The delay is the time needed to use up the fixed amount of thiosulfate.

questions.question: Oxidation of thiosulfate by hydrogen peroxide is thermodynamically favourable, but does not take place in the clock reaction. Suggest a reason.
questions.answer: The reaction has a high activation energy, so it is too slow to occur at the conditions used
steps: A reaction can be thermodynamically feasible (deltaG negative) but still have a very slow rate.
The oxidation of thiosulfate by hydrogen peroxide has a high activation energy.
Under the conditions of the clock reaction, very few collisions are energetic enough to react.
So the reaction does not compete measurably with the reduction of iodine by thiosulfate.

questions.question: The entropy change of the system for Reaction 1 is -43.8 J K-1 mol-1. With reference to the equation, suggest why it is negative.
questions.answer: Five moles of solid react to form three moles of solid, so the disorder decreases
steps: Reactants: SiO2(s) + 4Mg(s) = 5 moles of solid.
Products: Mg2Si(s) + 2MgO(s) = 3 moles of solid.
The number of moles of solids falls, so there are fewer ways to arrange the particles.
Solids have low entropy and there is no gas, so the disorder decreases and deltaS is negative.

questions.question: The enthalpy change for Reaction 1 is -370 kJ mol-1. Calculate the entropy change of the surroundings in J K-1 mol-1 at 23.0 C.
steps: Convert temperature: T = 23.0 + 273 = 296 K.
deltaS(surr) = -deltaH / T = -(-370 000 J mol-1) / 296 K.
deltaS(surr) = +1250 J K-1 mol-1.

questions.question: Calculate the total entropy change, deltaStotal, for Reaction 1 at 23.0 C, to an appropriate number of significant figures in J K-1 mol-1.
steps: deltaStotal = deltaSsystem + deltaSsurroundings.
deltaStotal = -43.8 + 1250 = +1206 J K-1 mol-1.

questions.question: Reaction 1 does not occur at room temperature because its activation energy is very high. Suggest why the activation energy is very high.
questions.answer: Strong covalent Si-O bonds in SiO2 must be broken, and the reaction is between solids with few points of contact
steps: SiO2 is a giant covalent structure with very strong Si-O bonds.
These strong bonds need a large amount of energy to break before the reaction can start.
Both reactants are solids, so there are few points of contact for collisions to occur.
Together these make the activation energy very high, so few collisions are successful at room temperature.

questions.question: Write an equation for the reaction of magnesium silicide, Mg2Si, with hydrochloric acid to form silane, SiH4, and magnesium chloride. State symbols are not required.
questions.answer: Mg2Si + 4HCl -> 2MgCl2 + SiH4
steps: Mg2Si gives 2 Mg atoms and 1 Si atom.
2 MgCl2 use 2 Mg and 4 Cl, so 4 HCl are needed.
SiH4 accounts for the Si and the 4 H atoms from the 4 HCl.
Balanced equation: Mg2Si + 4HCl -> 2MgCl2 + SiH4.

questions.question: Silane, SiH4, has a molecular structure. Complete the table giving the shape of a SiH4 molecule and its bond angle.
questions.answer: Tetrahedral; H-Si-H bond angle 109.5 degrees
steps: Silicon has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs of electrons around it.
The four pairs repel equally, so they arrange tetrahedrally (VSEPR).
The molecular shape is tetrahedral.
The H-Si-H bond angle is 109.5 degrees.
